name: End-grain wood engraving
summary: A burin cuts lines into a boxwood end-grain block, which is inked on the surface and printed with type. The cut becomes a white line on black, and fine parallel hatching gives the grey tones of Victorian magazines.

philosophy.core_thesis: A burin on the end grain of boxwood cuts white lines in a black block, so that fine tone and exact detail print with type.
design_principles: Think in white lines: each cut makes a white mark, and the uncut wood prints black.
Build tone with parallel cuts of 0.1–0.4 mm; widen the cuts to lighten a tone.
Use a tint tool to rule even grey skies and backgrounds, at about 100 lines an inch.
Print the block at type height, so that the picture sits in the text page with no join.
Keep the picture to one black ink; add colour only as a flat tint from a second block.
Join several blocks with bolts for a large picture, and place the joins in a quiet area.
anti_patterns: Gouge cuts with the coarse grain of a side-grain woodcut
Soft grey wash or a photographic tone
Thick contour lines with no fine hatching

process.matrix: Boxwood end-grain block, type height (about 23.3 mm)
process.press: Letterpress, platen or cylinder, often via electrotype
process.image_making: Burin and tint tools cut white lines; large blocks bolted from several pieces for double-page cuts

inks.strategy: One black letterpress ink, as for the text; the type and the picture print in the same pass.

screening.rule: Make a mid-tone with parallel white lines, 60–100 lines an inch; cross a second set at 60° only in the deepest shadow.

registration.rule: The block prints with the type in one pass, so no register is needed; a tint block can shift 0.3 mm.

substrate.stock: Machine-made wove paper or newsprint, off-white.
substrate.finish: Smooth wove, with a slight tooth from the machine felt.

surface.impression: A slight impression from the type pressure; the lines show on the back as a faint emboss.
surface.sheen: Matt black; a dense block can show a faint shine.
surface.texture: Very fine, even lines, with sharp edges and no grain from the wood.

evidence.title: (Horses) Waiting for Death
evidence.credit: Yale Center for British Art, via Wikimedia Commons

emotion.target_response: Exact, nineteenth-century trust: the viewer reads a news picture or a natural-history plate with precise detail.

use_cases: magazine and newspaper features with a period look
avoid_when: The image needs solid colour fields.
The look should be rough and hand-gouged.

modifiers.how: Use side-grain wood and a knife; cut thick lines and drop the fine tint lines.
Switch to copper and lines that swell; keep one black ink and a plate mark.
